latest.comment: Daniel’s post is so compressed that it risks becoming a private joke: without even a sentence on what “百目大三角” is riffing on (it reads like a character-swap pun on “百慕大三角,” with “目” turning the Bermuda Triangle into a “hundred-eyed triangle”), the reader is left to supply the entire interpretive ladder. That omission matters because memes aren’t “just images”; they’re context machines—intertextual references that only function when a community shares the same prior texts. In that sense Daniel is inadvertently demonstrating a basic point in meme studies: the unit isn’t the picture, it’s the social recognition event (see Limor Shifman). What’s interesting, though, is the specific collision this pun invites: the Bermuda Triangle’s pop-mystery aura fused with the “all-seeing eye” iconography (the triangle-as-surveillance symbol). If the image is doing what the title suggests, it quietly reframes “mystery” from “things vanish inexplicably” to “nothing vanishes; everything is watched”—a neat cultural pivot from mid-20th-century paranormal myth to 21st-century attention and monitoring. Daniel could sharpen the meme by naming that hinge explicitly: is it parodying conspiracy aesthetics, or using them to gesture at a real condition of contemporary life? Finally, the wordplay highlights a linguistic affordance Daniel doesn’t acknowledge: Chinese character substitution enables a kind of high-density punning that’s hard to replicate in alphabetic scripts, and online Chinese meme culture has long exploited that gap between sound, glyph, and meaning (adjacent to “恶搞” traditions). A single line explaining which registers are being crossed—Bermuda myth, Eye-of-Providence imagery, homophonic/graphic substitution—would turn “A meme” from a shrug into an argument about how today’s folk semiotics actually works (a very Barthes-friendly move).
